verses.1: Al-Mizan identifies the clear victory (fatḥ) with the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyyah. The sūrah’s promises to the Prophet and the faithful, its blame of the Bedouins, idolaters, and hypocrites, and its reference to a near victory (48:27) all concern the pilgrimage that produced the treaty. Though the journey exposed about fourteen hundred Muslims to a powerful, hostile Quraysh on its own ground, God turned the situation in their favour: Quraysh agreed to ten years’ cessation of hostilities, mutual security, and the Prophet’s return the following year with access to the Sanctuary and Kaʿbah for three days. The treaty enabled Islam’s spread and led toward the conquest of Mecca. Al-Mizan rejects identifying the verse directly with the conquest of Mecca or Khaybar, and finds a purely moral victory possible in itself but incompatible with the verses’ flow.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan argues that the apparent causal lām in lī yaghfira makes the usual senses of dhanb as disobedient sin and maghfirah as pardon unintelligible: victory has no intelligible connection with forgiving such sin. It therefore rejects the proposed oath-lām and the claim that forgiveness need not itself be connected with victory. Dhanb originally means an act with evil consequences, while maghfirah means covering; their familiar religious senses arose through usage. The Prophet’s call against faithlessness and idolatry had made the idolaters hostile, seeking revenge for their lost religion and leaders. God’s victory at Ḥudaybiyyah and the ensuing capture of Mecca removed their power, covering and removing these consequences. Thus the past and future dhanb are the consequences of his call before and after the Hijrah, as in Moses’ ‘charge’ in (62:14), not sins; the reading is supported by the promised completion of blessing and mighty help.

Al-Mizan rejects accounts of actual prophetic sins as contrary to Qur’an, Sunnah, reason, and prophetic ʿiṣmah, as well as still failing to connect pardon and victory. Promised forgiveness of future sins would suspend moral obligations and even encompass sins incompatible with the Prophet’s mission, contrary to (39:2), (39:12), and (69:44–46). Readings about Adam and Eve’s sins, the community’s sins through intercession, an implied ‘if you had sins,’ an honorific formula, or tark al-awlā and pragmatic directives either share the difficulty or fail to explain the causal connection. Sharīf al-Murtaḍā’s object-attributed dhanb, meaning the idolaters’ offence in expelling him and barring the Sanctuary, is close to Al-Mizan’s reading but departs slightly from the apparent wording. On Al-Mizan’s account, removal of those consequences prepares the truth’s victory, the Prophet’s guided course after Ḥudaybiyyah, and an exceptional divine help.

verses.4:
Al-Mizan defines sakīnah as the soul’s calm, steady tranquillity toward what it believes, identified with the spirit of faith mentioned in (2:248) and (58:22). God ‘sends it down’ by creating it in believers’ hearts from a lofty source, not by merely settling it there; this Qur’anic usage of inzāl also denotes origination. It rejects unsupported explanations of sakīnah as mercy, intellect, gravity, inclination to the Prophet’s message, an indwelling angel, or a creature with a cat’s head.

Al-Mizan holds that faith is knowledge joined to commitment to its practical implications, not knowledge alone, since knowledge can coexist with disbelief and apostasy, nor deeds alone, since deeds can coexist with hypocrisy. Both knowledge and commitment strengthen or weaken; therefore faith has real degrees, and sakīnah makes prior faith more complete. It rejects the view that faith is unchanging certain assent, whether its apparent increase is explained by continual renewal, by the growing number of revealed ordinances, by its effects alone, or by a distinction between innate and inferential faith. These accounts either confuse īmān with assent, leave qualitative differences in faith unexplained, or make the verse’s sending down of composure irrelevant. Persistence in good deeds strengthens faith and sins weaken it, as effects disclose their cause.

Al-Mizan reads God’s hosts as all visible and invisible immediate causes, obedient intermediaries between His will and its object. Their belonging to God explains His ability to send sakīnah and strengthen faith; His might and wisdom explain His disposal of those causes.
verses.5: Al-Mizan reads the admission of faithful men and women to abiding gardens and the absolution of their misdeeds as a further explanation of why God sent sakīnah: enhanced faith issues in paradise rather than punishment. The phrase may be syntactically linked in several ways, but this relation is clearest. Women are named alongside men to remove any impression, suggested by the jihād context, that paradise and absolution belong only to men. The abiding and absolution apply to both, and this is certain, true happiness because it is with God.
verses.6: Al-Mizan joins the punishment of hypocrites and polytheists to the faithful’s admission, naming hypocrites first because their harm to Muslims and punishment are greater (4:145). Their bad opinion of God is chiefly that He will not help His Messenger, though it may include every evil judgment of Him, including idolatry and disbelief. The adverse turn of fortune is either an invocation or a decree of destructive misfortune; wrath, curse, and hell complete the contrast with the faithful’s great success.
verses.7: Al-Mizan takes God’s possession of the hosts of heaven and earth, and His might and wisdom, to explain both the promised admission of faithful men and women and the punishment of hypocrites and polytheists. The alternative that it is solely a threat, reminding the latter that they remain within His power, is less suited to the verse’s apparent meaning.
verses.8: Al-Mizan says the Prophet witnesses deeds of faith, faithlessness, righteousness, and vice in this world and bears witness in the next; he brings good news of nearness to God and abundant reward to the faithful and Godwary, and warns disbelievers and those who turn away of painful punishment. The sending has the purpose that people believe in God and His Messenger, support, revere, and glorify God, including through prayer morning and evening. Although the common recitation addresses ‘you,’ the third-person recitation of Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr better fits the context. Al-Mizan takes the harmonious pronouns in support, reverence, and glorification all to refer to God, rejecting the division that makes the first two refer to the Messenger and the last to God.

verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains bayʿah as a pledge of obedience in matters within the ruler’s authority, named from a sale’s handclasp because it symbolizes transfer of the right of disposal. Pledging allegiance to the Prophet is therefore pledging allegiance to God: obedience offered to him is offered to God. ‘The hand of God is above their hands’ intensifies this identity, making the Prophet’s hand God’s hand in the same sense that his throwing is ascribed to God in (8:17); it also appears that the Prophet’s hand lay above theirs. Breaking the pledge consequently harms only its breaker, while fulfilling God’s covenant brings a great reward, for God needs no one.

Al-Mizan finds the metaphorical reading that represents God as another participant in the pledge appropriate only if it avoids imagining a form from which God is transcendent. It rejects readings of ‘hand’ as divine power and assistance, or as gifts, reward, or guidance, because these are foreign to the context’s magnification of allegiance to the Prophet; other unsupported readings likewise fail.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains al-mukhallafūn as those left behind and al-aʿrāb as Bedouin Arabs rather than settled Arabs. The verse foretells, apparently before the Prophet reached Medina from Ḥudaybiyyah, their claim that possessions and families detained them and their request for forgiveness. Their wording acknowledges that staying behind was sinful, but God exposes both the excuse and request as speech not held in their hearts, intended only to escape blame.

Even taking their excuse as true, Al-Mizan reads the reply as showing that property and family cannot ward off harm or procure benefit against the will of the sole sovereign, God. Worldly means may be used where God commands them, but not when they conflict with the higher priority of defending the Truth, even at risk, unless there is certain danger that makes the effort futile. God’s knowledge of their deeds is thus a subtle warning that their stated excuse was a lie.
verses.12: Al-Mizan says the Bedouins’ real reason for staying behind was their expectation that the Messenger and faithful would be killed by Quraysh and never return, not concern for their families or wealth. Satan made that thought attractive, and they acted on it by refusing to go. Their evil opinion may mean this expectation itself, but Al-Mizan finds it closer to the wording that they thought God would not support His Messenger or make His religion prevail.
verses.13: Al-Mizan treats joining faith in God to faith in His Messenger as proof that disobeying the Messenger is disbelief in God. The prepared, indefinite ‘blaze’ is a threatening roaring inferno; using ‘the faithless’ rather than a pronoun makes their disbelief the stated reason for that rule and heightens its terror.
verses.14: Al-Mizan says God’s absolute kingdom confirms the preceding warning: He forgives whom He wishes and punishes whom He wishes. Appending ghafūr and raḥīm to that dominion indicates that His mercy precedes His wrath and encourages the hearer to seek forgiveness and mercy.
verses.15: Al-Mizan identifies the foretold expedition for booty as Khaybar. Those who stayed behind at Ḥudaybiyyah will seek to join for wealth, but God had promised Khaybar’s spoils to those who accompanied the Prophet there, so the command excludes everyone else. Their charge that the believers are merely envious rejects the Prophet’s divinely commanded statement and supposes that he withholds booty for himself and his companions. Al-Mizan therefore reads ‘they understand but a little’ as describing their simple-minded inability to understand what is said, not partial comprehension or merely a minority’s ignorance; such a claim to the Messenger itself displays their weak minds.
verses.16: Al-Mizan holds that the Bedouins will later be summoned against a mighty people whom the Prophet fought after Khaybar, plausibly including Hawāzin, Thaqīf, or the Romans at Muʾtah; the alternatives include apostates, and others. ‘They will embrace Islam, or you will fight them’ opens two alternatives and indicates polytheists who are not offered jizyah like the People of the Book: they must accept Islam or be fought. It rejects reading ‘you will fight them’ as an adjective of ‘a people,’ since the summons is to fight them. Going forth earns a good reward; turning away as at Ḥudaybiyyah brings painful punishment, apparently in this world, though possibly in both worlds.
verses.17: Al-Mizan takes the removal of ḥaraj, toil, from the blind, lame, and sick as exemption from the general duty of jihād for conditions that make it difficult. The verse then restates the preceding rule: obedience to God and His Messenger brings gardens with running streams, while refusal brings painful punishment.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan says God’s riḍā, unlike a fleeting state in a soul, is an Attribute of Act: His good recompense for an action. Although it is phrased as pleasure in persons, it is attached to their act of pledging allegiance beneath the umbrella-thorn tree at Ḥudaybiyyah. What God knew in their hearts was not everything in them but their sincere, dedicated intention in that pledge; readings of faith and love of religion, or distress at the treaty, do not fit the tone.

The apparent sequence—God was pleased, then knew—does not reverse causation. As an Attribute of Act, divine pleasure is manifested through the whole connected reality of His knowledge of their intention, His sending sakīnah, and His recompense. The near victory and abundant spoils are Khaybar and its spoils, not the conquest of Mecca. God’s might means His will prevails, and His wisdom means He acts purposefully.

verses.20:
Al-Mizan takes the abundant spoils as Khaybar and later expeditions, while ‘this one’ is the imminent spoils of Khaybar promised in the preceding verse; the claim that it means the pledge beneath the tree is weak. The sūrah was most commonly held to have been revealed while the Prophet returned from Ḥudaybiyyah, though an after-Khaybar revelation would make the phrase straightforward. Reports variously identify the people whose hands God withheld as Asad and Ghatafān threatening Muslim families in Medina, their forces coming to aid Khaybar, or the Meccans and their allies who accepted a treaty.

These fulfilled promises and the sūrah’s other prophecies are a sign that the faithful are upon truth, that God’s promise is true, and that the Prophet is truthful. The straight path is the course that exalts Truth and spreads religion, rather than merely trust and reliance in every action.
verses.21: Al-Mizan reads the verse as promising other, not-yet-captured spoils encompassed by God’s power. Competing grammatical accounts that join ‘others’ to the prior spoils, make it the object of an implicit decree, or supply an implicit rubba are all weak. It prefers the spoils of Hawāzin; Persia and Rome, or an unmentioned town identified with Mecca, are alternative readings.
verses.22: Al-Mizan presents this as good news that faithless opponents cannot withstand the faithful alone: they will flee and find neither a protector to manage their affairs nor an Arab helper willing to assist them.
verses.23: Al-Mizan says God’s unchanging precedent is to grant victory to His Prophets and their faithful followers over faithless enemies, provided they are true in faith and sincere in intention, as in (58:21). Muslim military reversals therefore arise only through contravening God and His Prophet, not through a change in that precedent.
verses.24: Al-Mizan identifies the mutual withholding of hands in the valley of Mecca with the Treaty of Ḥudaybiyyah. Quraysh, reinforced by Abyssinians, had assembled for conflict; the faithful had pledged to fight and the Prophet had resolved to confront them. Yet after God had given the Prophet and faithful the advantage of occupying their enemies’ territory, He prevented battle and restrained each side. Ḥudaybiyyah is called the valley of Mecca because of its nearness to it, perhaps even within the Sanctuary’s land.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan says the Meccan idolaters barred the believers from the Sacred Mosque and detained the ʿUmrah offerings, which should have been slaughtered in Mecca; the pilgrims were in iḥrām for that purpose. God withheld the believers from them because unknown faithful men and women remained among the Meccans: otherwise the Muslims might unknowingly kill them and incur blame and harm. The implicit consequence is that, absent this danger, God would not have restrained them.

He thereby admits those hidden believers to mercy by preserving them and admits the Muslims to mercy by preserving them from blame. The alternative confines that mercy to later converts among the disbelievers. Had the faithful and faithless inhabitants of Mecca been distinguishable, God would have punished the faithless among them; their presence among the idolaters prevented that punishment.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan defines ḥamiyyah as the inflamed faculty of anger and takes the faithless’ ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyyah as belligerence rooted in pagan religion. ‘Put’ means cast into their hearts, and the repeated designation ‘the faithless’ states the reason for the judgment. The temporal clause most naturally relates to their barring the believers, rather than to the threatened punishment or an implied command to remember.

God countered their belligerence by sending sakīnah upon the Messenger and faithful, calming them and preventing rash action. He made them abide by the word of Godwariness. While it has been read as Divine Unity, steadfastness in the pledge, or sakīnah, Al-Mizan considers it likely to be the spirit of faith (rūḥ al-īmān), which impels Godwariness; the alleged pledge in the World of Particles is rejected as foolish. They were worthiest of this gift through their righteous preparation and its exclusive recipients; God’s knowledge encompasses all.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan reads ‘God has fulfilled His Messenger’s vision in all truth’ as a sworn assurance that the faithful will enter the Sacred Mosque, God willing, safe, shaven or cropped, and without fear. The divine qualification teaches that all things depend on His will. ‘Besides that’ means before that entry: God knew the benefit unknown to them and appointed the near victory of Ḥudaybiyyah to make their peaceful ʿUmrah possible. Without the treaty and its clauses they could enter only through fighting and bloodshed, incompatible with ʿUmrah.

The verse therefore answers companions who assumed the vision meant entry that year and doubted it when Quraysh stopped them at Ḥudaybiyyah. It affirms that the God-given vision was true but deferred for a year. Al-Mizan rejects the reading that the near victory is Khaybar, and finds the conquest of Mecca still further from the context.
verses.28: Al-Mizan refers to its earlier explanation of the Messenger’s guidance and true religion prevailing over every religion. It takes God’s sufficiency as witness either to the truth of the Prophet’s mission and that promise, or to the truth of the preceding vision.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan describes those with Muḥammad as hard against the faithless yet merciful among themselves; the second quality prevents their hardness from implying harshness toward fellow believers. Their continual bowing and prostration means regular prayer, seeking God’s reward and riḍwān; their facial mark is the visible sign of Godwariness produced by humble prostration. A narration from Imām al-Ṣādiq identifies it with wakefulness in prayer. Al-Mizan does not adopt the alternatives of forehead dust from prostrating on soil or a luminous Resurrection-day mark.

Their description appears in the Torah and Injīl. Al-Mizan first takes both scriptural references to describe the listed qualities, while allowing the alternative that the Injīl’s separate similitude is a tillage whose fresh shoots it supports until they become stout, firm stalks that impress sowers. The image signifies the believers’ increasing number, power, and preparedness, which enrages the faithless.

The promise of forgiveness and great reward is, however, for those among them who continue in faith and righteous deeds. Al-Mizan reads min as partitive, not expository, because an expository min does not govern a pronoun. Thus undisclosed hypocrites, later apostates, and believers lacking righteous conduct are excluded; the conditions of (48:10), Ibn ʿAbbās’s report that sakīnah was sent only upon those known to fulfil the pledge, and (24:55) reinforce this. It rejects the claim that the promise covers every companion, including an argument from continuous prayer, since that describes their past and present rather than their future. Unconditional future forgiveness would annul moral obligations and accountability, which is impossible; even the infallible prophets’ deeds would not avail them if they ascribed partners to God (6:88).
